opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the predictor is really the piece that gets closest to what we mean by a world model. In V-JEPA, the encoder learns representations of video, but the predictor's job is to take the representation of what's visible, some context, and predict the representation of what's been masked out, either in space or in time. That's essentially asking it to build an internal model of how the world fills in: how objects persist, how things move, what's likely to happen next.

The key distinction from a lot of generative approaches is that we're predicting in representation space, not pixel space. The world is full of unpredictable detail, like the exact texture of leaves blowing or noise in the background. If you force a model to reconstruct every pixel, it spends a lot of capacity on things that don't matter for understanding or acting. By predicting in an abstract space, the predictor can focus on the predictable, semantically meaningful parts of the scene and just discard the rest.

So the way I see it, the current predictor is a step toward a world model, but not the full thing yet. Right now it's mostly used as a training signal: it shapes the encoder to learn good features, and then for downstream tasks we often just freeze the encoder and probe it. The next step is making the predictor useful in its own right. That means conditioning it on actions, so that given the current state and an action, it can predict the future state. Once you have that, you can start doing planning: imagine different action sequences in latent space, evaluate where they lead, and pick the one that gets you closer to a goal. That's where it becomes a world model in the sense Yann and others have described, something an agent can use to reason about the consequences of its actions before taking them.

There are open challenges too. Predicting over longer time horizons, handling uncertainty when several futures are plausible, and building hierarchy so you can predict at different levels of abstraction and time scales. But I think the basic recipe of learning a predictor in a learned representation space, from lots of unlabeled video, is a really promising foundation for getting there.

r001.rationale: It names handling uncertainty across plausible futures as an open challenge, but does not identify uncertainty modeling as an ability of the predictor that advances a world model.

r002.rationale: It says the next step is to make the predictor useful in its own right by conditioning it on actions and using it to plan.

r003.rationale: It does not compare how standardized the evaluation of predictors or world models is with evaluation of learned representations.

r004.rationale: It mentions building a hierarchy for predictions at different abstraction levels, but not having the predictor autonomously choose a perceptual representation level for the agent’s current task.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that the predictor is really the piece of the system that's doing the "modeling" part of world modeling. The encoder gives you a representation of what you're seeing, but the predictor is the thing that has to say, given what I've observed so far, what's going to happen in the parts of the video I haven't seen, or in the frames that come next. And crucially, it's doing that in representation space, not pixel space. So it doesn't have to predict every leaf blowing in the wind or the exact texture of a surface. It can focus on the predictable, high-level structure of the scene, which is really the stuff you'd want a world model to capture anyway.

So in the V-JEPA setup, the predictor is trained in a fairly simple way. You mask out large regions of the video in space and time, and the predictor has to fill in the representations of those missing regions from the context it does get to see. What's interesting is that even with that pretty constrained objective, the predictor ends up learning things that look a lot like intuitive physics. You can show it videos where objects do physically implausible things, like an object disappearing behind an occluder and never coming back, and the predictor's error spikes. It's essentially surprised. That's exactly the kind of behavior you want from a world model: it should have expectations about how the world unfolds, and it should be able to tell you when those expectations are violated.

Now, where I think it becomes a real step toward a world model, rather than just a nice self-supervised pretraining trick, is when you make the predictor conditional on actions. In V-JEPA 2, for example, we take the frozen encoder and train a predictor that's conditioned on what a robot arm is doing, so it can predict how the representation of the scene changes as a function of the action. And once you have that, you can do planning. You take your current observation, you take a goal image, and you search over sequences of actions by rolling the predictor forward and asking which sequence gets the predicted representation closest to the goal. That's model-predictive control, essentially, but in a learned latent space, and it works zero-shot on robots the model has never seen during the action-conditioned training.

So I'd put it this way: the predictor is the component that carries the predictive, causal, "what happens if" knowledge. The encoder is about perception, the predictor is about dynamics. And the long-term vision is that you scale this up, you make the predictions hierarchical so you can reason over longer horizons and at multiple levels of abstraction, and you make it the core of an agent that can plan and reason about the physical world without having to be explicitly trained on every task. We're nowhere near done. There's a lot to figure out around long-horizon prediction, around memory, around how uncertainty gets represented in latent space. But I do think the predictor is the right abstraction to be building that on.

r001.rationale: The response says representing uncertainty in latent space remains an open problem; it does not claim the predictor can model uncertainty.

r002.rationale: It describes using the trained predictor to roll forward candidate action sequences for planning toward a goal.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare how standardized evaluation is for predictors or world models versus learned representations.

r004.rationale: It mentions hierarchical predictions at multiple abstraction levels, but not a predictor autonomously choosing the perceptual representation suited to the current task.

astra-6.text:
I think of the predictor as a step toward learning how the world evolves. If you observe part of a video, can you predict the representation of what you haven’t seen? The idea is that you don’t necessarily need to generate every pixel to learn something useful about the underlying dynamics. You want to predict at a level of abstraction that captures what matters, without having to account for every unpredictable visual detail.

To move toward a world model, you’d want to extend that to predictions conditioned on actions: given the current state and an action I might take, what happens next? Then you could potentially use those predictions to compare actions and plan. So I see the V-JEPA predictor as a building block for that, rather than a complete world model on its own. The question is whether the representations and the predictive structure we learn from video can support that next step.

r001.rationale: The response mentions unpredictable visual detail and abstract predictions, but does not say the predictor models uncertainty.

r002.rationale: It describes the predictor as a building block for action-conditioned prediction and planning, but does not clearly advocate continuing to use the trained predictor.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison between how standardized evaluations are for predictors or world models versus learned representations.

r004.rationale: It discusses predicting at an abstract level, but does not propose that the model choose a perceptual representation suited to the agent’s current task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of the predictor as a first step toward learning how the world evolves in an abstract representation space. The idea is that you don’t necessarily need to predict every pixel in a future video frame. You want to predict the things that matter, while being able to ignore details that are inherently unpredictable.

For a world model, you’d eventually want to condition those predictions on actions: given what I know about the world right now, if I take this action, what happens next? That could let an agent evaluate possible actions in its representation space before actually executing them.

So I’d view the V-JEPA predictor as a building block. Learning predictive representations from video is an important step, but connecting that to actions and planning is what would make it useful as a world model.

r001.rationale: The response says the predictor can ignore details that are inherently unpredictable, but does not state that it models uncertainty.

r002.rationale: It calls the predictor a building block and describes future action-conditioned planning, but does not advocate using the predictor after training.

r003.rationale: The response makes no comparison between how predictors or world models and learned representations are evaluated.

r004.rationale: It discusses predicting relevant features in abstract representation space, but does not propose that the predictor autonomously choose the perceptual representation level based on the agent’s current task.
